target.title: fix(process): add gemini and claude to Windows .cmd shim allowlist
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

- On Windows, using the `google-gemini-cli` provider fails with `spawn gemini ENOENT` because Node's `child_process.spawn` does not automatically resolve `.cmd` extensions (only `.exe`/`.com`)
- npm global installs on Windows create `.cmd` shim files, so `gemini` (and `claude`) need the `.cmd` suffix to be found by `spawn`
- Fixes #98573

## Why This Change Was Made

The supervisor child adapter (`src/process/supervisor/adapters/child.ts`) has a `resolveCommand` function that uses `resolveWindowsCommandShim` with a hardcoded allowlist of commands that should get `.cmd` appended on Windows. The list included `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, and `npx` but not `gemini` or `claude` — so spawning those CLI tools failed on Windows.

## What Was Changed

- Added `gemini` and `claude` to the `cmdCommands` allowlist in `src/process/supervisor/adapters/child.ts:26`
- This triggers the same `.cmd` resolution + `cmd.exe` wrapping mechanism already used and verified for `pnpm`, `yarn`, `npm`, and `npx`

## Scope

This PR is intentionally narrow: **allowlist-only**. The shared `cmd.exe` metacharacter escaping change has been split out to a follow-up PR to keep the shell-boundary review separate from the shim resolution fix.

## User Impact

- Windows users can now use the `google-gemini-cli` and `claude-cli` providers without encountering `ENOENT` spawn errors
- No change on macOS or Linux (platform guard already skips non-Windows)
- No change to the shared `cmd.exe` escaping path (metacharacter rejection behavior is unchanged)

## Evidence

### Real Windows Machine (MINGW64, Node.js v22.19.0)

**Bug:** `spawn("gemini") -> ENOENT`, `spawn("gemini.cmd") -> EINVAL` (CVE-2024-27980)  
**Fix:** `cmd.exe /d /s /c "gemini.cmd --version" -> exit 0`

### npm package evidence
`@google/gemini-cli` declares `{"gemini":"bundle/gemini.js"}` -> Windows npm creates `gemini.cmd`

### CI evidence
- `checks-windows-node-test` on `windows-latest`: all process tests pass on real Windows
- All unit tests pass via `setPlatform("win32")` simulation

## Tests

```bash
pnpm test src/process/supervisor/adapters/child.test.ts  # 21 tests, 20 pass (1 pre-existing Linux failure)
pnpm test src/process/windows-command.test.ts  # 4 tests pass
```

New tests added:
- `wraps gemini CLI command through trusted cmd.exe on Windows (#98573)` — verifies `gemini` -> `gemini.cmd` wrapped via `cmd.exe`
- `wraps claude CLI command through trusted cmd.exe on Windows` — same for `claude`
- `keeps gemini command unchanged on non-Windows platforms (#98573)` — verifies no `.cmd` suffix on Linux

## Risk checklist

- [x] No: Does this change affect user-visible behavior? (Only affects Windows CLI tool spawning, restoring expected behavior)
- [x] No: Does this change affect configuration surface?
- [x] No: Does this change affect security? (No change to security model; same allowlist pattern used for other CLI tools like pnpm/npm/yarn)
- [x] No: Does this change affect plugin APIs?
- [x] No: Does this change require documentation updates?

target.title: fix: harden formatCurrencyAmount, formatCoords, and record code-mode bridge rejections
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Three defensive hardening changes across location formatting, DeepSeek usage formatting, and code-mode bridge promise handling. The gateway-lock handle leak has been dropped (covered by #98848).

## Why This Change Was Made

### 1. Record rejected code-mode bridge promises at pending-state creation boundary

`createPendingBridgeStates` attached a fulfillment-only `.then((settled) => state.settled = settled)` to each bridge promise. A rejection would surface as unhandledRejection.

**Fix:** `.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)` records `{ ok: false, error }` in entry.settled at creation time.

### 2. Guard `formatCurrencyAmount` against non-finite amounts

`formatCurrencyAmount` calls `amount.toFixed(2)` without `Number.isFinite`. NaN produces "$NaN".

### 3. Guard `formatCoords` against NaN/Infinity coordinates

`formatCoords` calls `latitude.toFixed(6)` without `Number.isFinite`. NaN renders as "NaN, NaN".

## User Impact

- **code-mode**: Prevents unhandledRejection from late-rejecting bridge promises. Error preserved in settled state.
- **DeepSeek/location**: Defensive hardening — "unknown" instead of misleading "NaN"/"Infinity".

## Evidence

### Real OpenClaw runtime terminal output

## What Problem This Solves

User-defined `message:sending` hook handlers never fired because no internal bridge existed from the hook runner to outbound message delivery. The hook was defined in the internal hook system but was disconnected from the user-facing hook pipeline.

## Root Cause

The `message:sending` internal hook was emitted via `emitInternalEvent()` in `src/infra/outbound/deliver.ts` but the user-defined hook pipeline (`src/hooks/internal-hooks.ts`) never subscribed to or forwarded this event.

## Fix

Wire `message:sending` from the internal hook emitter to the user-defined hook pipeline so that hook handlers registered via `[hooks]` configuration receive `message:sending` events before outbound message delivery. Hook handlers can observe, transform, or suppress messages.

target.title: Add native Signal reply quotes
target.body:
## Summary

Signal auto-replies now preserve native Signal quote context when OpenClaw responds to the inbound Signal message that triggered the turn. The Signal plugin carries the inbound message timestamp, author, and body through reply delivery, sends quote metadata to native `signal-cli`/json-rpc, and maps the same quote fields to the Signal REST container send API. If quote metadata is missing, explicitly disabled, aimed at a different reply target, or rejected by the backend, OpenClaw falls back to a normal Signal message instead of dropping the reply.

## What Changed

- Inbound Signal handling records the inbound timestamp as the current reply target and carries native quote context into reply delivery.
- Signal text and media auto-replies include `replyToId`, `replyToAuthor`, and `replyToBody` only when they match the triggering inbound message.
- `replyToCurrent: false`, mismatched explicit reply targets, `replyToMode: off`, and single-message `batched` mode suppress native quote metadata for implicit replies.
- `replyToMode: first` consumes native quote metadata only for the first normal implicit reply; `replyToMode: all` preserves it across each emitted reply chunk.
- Explicit current-message replies can still quote the current message even when implicit reply mode is off.
- Native sends retry without quote metadata when Signal rejects quote fields, including unrecognized quote-field errors, while receipts preserve `replyToId` and record whether native quote send used `sent` or `fallback` status.
- Signal REST container mode translates quote metadata to `/v2/send` snake_case fields and strips `uuid:` prefixes from quote authors for the container API.
- Signal config now accepts `replyToMode` and direct/group `replyToModeByChatType` at channel and account scope, with account values taking precedence over channel chat-type overrides.
- Signal approval-reaction hint registration handles structured approval payload delivery, UUID-only linked accounts, and icon-prefixed approval prompt headers while preserving the current `signal.approval-reactions.v2` persistence namespace.
- Signal docs describe native quote behavior, fallback, and the new reply-to config fields.

## Proof

Behavioral proof:

- Focused automated coverage proves native quote send, fallback retry, receipt metadata, REST container quote fields, UUID author normalization, inbound context wiring, text replies, media replies, mismatched reply-target suppression, `replyToCurrent: false`, explicit current-message quoting, `replyToMode` chat/account precedence, single-use quote consumption, all-mode multi-chunk quoting, approval-reaction registration, and config schema acceptance/rejection.
- Live Signal proof used a local Signal REST/json-rpc linked device. A non-self inbound event in the Testing realm group was captured, the feature-branch send path sent one quoted proof reply with `replyToId`, `replyToAuthor`, and `replyToBody`, Signal accepted the send with `deliveredMessageIdPresent=true`, and Jesse visually confirmed the reply appeared in Signal.

Manual proof gaps and follow-up risks:

- The live proof covers group native quote delivery. Basic Signal DM reply behavior is already working in this linked setup, but this closeout did not add a fresh manual DM native-quote proof.
- No further live Signal messages were sent after the confirmed Testing realm proof.
- Temporary local Signal REST/container config fixes used to complete live proof are not product proof and are not part of this PR.
- Signal group id normalization and Signal mention matching remain separate follow-up risks outside this PR.

Screenshots are not included because this is a backend channel transport change with no OpenClaw-rendered UI surface. The human-visible proof is the live Signal confirmation above.

## Verification

target.title: fix(agents): Anthropic replay fails after boundaryless compaction
target.body:
Related: #30157

## What Problem This Solves

Anthropic/Bedrock signed-thinking replay can fail after a compacted session is rotated into a successor transcript that no longer carries a `compactionSummary` message. Those successor transcripts may still replay pre-compaction assistant thinking signatures, but the signatures are bound to the old context prefix and can be rejected by the provider.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing stale-signature cleanup only had the in-transcript compaction summary timestamp available. This change recovers a conservative compaction timestamp for legacy boundaryless successor transcripts by looking at the parent session metadata when:

- the current replay has no `compactionSummary`,
- the session header points at a parent transcript,
- the parent compaction predates the successor session,
- the active child branch contains the parent compaction's `firstKeptEntryId`, and
- the child branch is missing an ancestor before that kept entry, which distinguishes rotated compacted successors from ordinary forks.

The parent transcript scan is bounded to files up to 64 MiB and cached by file snapshot, so normal parented sessions do not rescan large parents on every replay. If the boundary cannot be proven, replay behavior stays unchanged.

## Scope

This is a narrow boundaryless-successor repair under the broader signed-thinking replay cluster. It does not claim to close every Anthropic/Bedrock signed-thinking replay failure path; it only handles legacy successor transcripts whose compaction boundary can be proven from the parent transcript.

## User Impact

Users can continue affected legacy compacted Anthropic/Bedrock sessions without manually disabling truncation, resetting the session, or losing the visible replay tail. Normal forks, sessions without parent compaction, post-compaction signed thinking, and latest interrupted assistant recovery remain preserved.

## Real behavior proof

Live Anthropic replay proof was run against PR head `9d2565bc03519e02e63a1017b2ac8a67019651be` with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` loaded from a local `.env`; the key was not printed. The proof builds a boundaryless successor transcript with a stale pre-compaction thinking signature, confirms the unsanitized replay is rejected by Anthropic, then sends the sanitized OpenClaw replay through the real Anthropic transport.

target.title: fix: sSH transport security check rejects connection before tunnel is established
target.body:
Closes #26250

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users configuring a remote Gateway with SSH transport could be rejected by the plaintext `ws://` security check before OpenClaw had a chance to establish the configured SSH tunnel.

The affected workflow is the documented remote Gateway setup using `gateway.mode: "remote"`, `gateway.remote.url`, and `gateway.remote.sshTarget`. In that setup, the configured Gateway URL may point at the remote endpoint, but the runtime connection is expected to go through a local SSH-forwarded endpoint.

- Behavior or issue addressed: Configured remote Gateway SSH transport (`transport: "ssh"`, or omitted `transport` with `sshTarget`) now reaches the managed SSH tunnel path before the raw non-loopback `ws://` URL is rejected. The review follow-up around malformed or non-Gateway configured URLs is also addressed: those configs stay on the fail-closed validation path instead of being rewritten into a loopback fallback.
- Root cause: The Gateway connection resolver and SSH tunnel rewrite path did not share a strict source-of-truth validation boundary for config-owned SSH transport. The resolver needed to recognize only config-derived managed SSH remotes before the generic plaintext guard, while the tunnel starter also needed to parse and validate the configured Gateway websocket URL before any SSH process or loopback rewrite could occur.

## Why This Change Was Made

The change keeps the plaintext safety check strict for direct connections, CLI/env URL overrides, and SSH configs without `sshTarget`, while allowing config-derived SSH remotes to be classified as managed SSH transport before the raw remote URL is rejected. The owning Gateway call/bootstrap paths start the SSH tunnel, rewrite the runtime websocket URL to `127.0.0.1:<localPort>`, and stop the tunnel when the call finishes or the long-lived client shuts down or fails during startup.

Malformed or non-Gateway configured SSH remote URLs still fail closed: the SSH exception only applies after the configured URL parses as an accepted Gateway websocket URL, and tunnel startup no longer rewrites malformed config into a loopback fallback.

- Fix classification: Root-cause fix for the configured SSH Gateway transport validation and lifecycle boundary.
- Why this is root-cause fix: The fix moves the exception to the correct contract boundary instead of weakening the plaintext guard. Only config-derived remote Gateway URLs that parse as `ws:` or `wss:`, use SSH transport semantics, and include `sshTarget` can enter the managed SSH path; malformed URLs, non-websocket URLs, CLI/env overrides, direct transport, and missing `sshTarget` continue through the normal security validation and fail closed when unsafe.
- Patch quality notes: The patch keeps the change scoped to Gateway connection resolution, configured SSH tunnel startup, and the call/bootstrap clients that own tunnel lifecycle. It avoids broad probe/status rewrites and adds regression coverage at both the resolver boundary and tunnel-start boundary.
- Architecture / source-of-truth check: The source of truth is the Gateway remote config contract plus the managed SSH tunnel owner. `transport: "direct"` remains the explicit opt-out, omitted `transport` with `sshTarget` remains the documented SSH default, and the runtime URL is only rewritten after the configured Gateway websocket URL has been parsed and accepted.
- Related open PR / same-contract scan: This updates the existing PR #96134 for issue #26250 rather than opening a competing PR. The same-contract scan for this update is limited to the configured remote Gateway SSH transport path and the clients that consume `resolveGatewayClientBootstrap`.
- What did NOT change: This intentionally does not change status, health, doctor, TUI, security-audit, logs, devices, or Crestodian probe behavior; it also does not add WSS-over-SSH SNI behavior, reconnect tunnel restart behavior, schema changes, migrations, or a new transport protocol.
- Out of scope: Non-owning Gateway probes and broader remote Gateway product decisions remain out of scope for this focused PR. The only maintainer-decision boundary called out here is whether the configured SSH allowance should remain limited to config-derived remote Gateway URLs with `sshTarget`.

## User Impact

Users following the configured SSH remote Gateway path can connect through the managed tunnel instead of seeing an early plaintext `ws://` rejection. Explicit unsafe plaintext remotes still fail closed unless they are owned by the configured SSH tunnel path, so credentials and chat data remain protected from accidental direct plaintext network use.

The main compatibility point for reviewers is that configs with `gateway.remote.sshTarget` and omitted `gateway.remote.transport` continue to use the documented SSH default. Maintainers should also review the security boundary around when the pre-tunnel plaintext allowance applies.

- Why it matters / User impact: The documented SSH remote Gateway setup becomes usable without weakening the protection against accidental plaintext remote Gateway connections.
- Maintainer-ready confidence: High after focused red/green regression tests, a real local OpenSSH behavior proof, the Gateway-focused suite, core type tests, and a final diff scan against `origin/main`.
- Risk labels considered: Security boundary, networking, Gateway lifecycle, and SSH process cleanup.
- Risk explanation: The highest-risk area is accidentally allowing a direct plaintext remote URL or leaking an SSH tunnel process. The patch narrows the SSH exception to config-owned managed transport and wires cleanup through one-shot calls, long-lived clients, and startup failure paths.
- Why acceptable: The risk is acceptable because direct transport, CLI/env overrides, malformed URLs, non-websocket URLs, and configs without `sshTarget` remain rejected; regression tests cover those boundaries, and the real behavior proof shows the configured SSH path succeeds while an explicit unsafe `--url` override still fails.

## Evidence

- Which bot or reviewer comments were addressed: The ClawSweeper comment asking for malformed configured SSH remote URLs to stay fail-closed is addressed by validating configured Gateway websocket URLs before granting the SSH exception and before starting the SSH tunnel. The broader probe/status concerns remain intentionally unchanged because they are outside issue #26250's configured SSH transport scope.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: Focused Gateway SSH tests, the broader Gateway client/call/bootstrap suite, SSH tunnel infra tests, ACP startup tests, MCP channel bridge tests, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`, `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD`, and a real local OpenSSH configured-SSH behavior proof were run after the patch.
- Evidence after fix: The focused regression tests cover malformed URLs, non-websocket URLs, direct transport, missing `sshTarget`, omitted SSH transport defaulting, tunnel startup, and tunnel cleanup. The real behavior proof used a non-loopback configured Gateway URL plus a managed local SSH forward.
- Observed result after fix: Configured SSH Gateway calls succeeded through the managed loopback tunnel, explicit unsafe `--url` override failed with the expected security error, the OpenSSH daemon observed public-key auth and direct-tcpip forwarding, no leftover OpenClaw SSH forward process remained, and all listed validation commands passed except the unrelated full `pnpm check:test-types` attempt noted below.
- What was not tested: A full `pnpm check:test-types` run was attempted but is not claimed as passing because it failed only in unrelated `extensions/qa-lab` type errors outside this PR's touched files. Remote hosted SSH infrastructure, WSS-over-SSH SNI behavior, reconnect tunnel restart behavior, and non-owning status/health/doctor probe changes were not tested because they are outside this PR's scope.
- Target test file: `src/gateway/ssh-transport.test.ts`, `src/gateway/call.test.ts`, `src/gateway/client-bootstrap.test.ts`, `src/gateway/client.test.ts`, `src/gateway/operator-approvals-client.test.ts`, `src/infra/ssh-tunnel.test.ts`, `src/acp/server.startup.test.ts`, and `src/mcp/channel-bridge.test.ts`.
- Scenario locked in: A configured remote Gateway with SSH transport can connect via the managed local tunnel; malformed or non-websocket configured SSH remote URLs reject before SSH startup; direct transport and explicit CLI/env URL overrides do not get the configured SSH allowance.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: The regression tests pin the two source boundaries where the bug can recur: connection-detail classification before the plaintext guard, and tunnel-start URL validation before SSH process creation and loopback rewrite. That is narrower and more reliable than adding broad probe behavior changes or relaxing the security guard globally.

Focused validation run after the patch, including the malformed `gateway.remote.url` fail-closed regression coverage:

target.title: fix(config): allow Nix-mode doctor --fix for non-config writes
target.body:
## Summary

Fix Nix-mode write guard blocking `openclaw doctor --fix` / `--repair` / `--yes` when the repair work does not modify `openclaw.json`, while keeping `--generate-gateway-token` fail-fast because it necessarily mutates config.

## What Problem This Solves

When `OPENCLAW_NIX_MODE=1`, `assertConfigWriteAllowedInCurrentMode()` was invoked unconditionally at the start of the doctor flow for `--fix`, `--repair`, `--yes`, and `--generate-gateway-token`. That blocked repairs that do not actually modify `openclaw.json`:

1. **`openclaw doctor --fix` / `--repair` / `--yes`** - Refused to run even when the only pending repairs were session state fixes, legacy state migrations, or permission fixes (none of which touch `openclaw.json`).

## Why This Change Was Made

The Nix-mode write guard should only block operations that actually mutate `openclaw.json`. Doctor repairs that write to other stores (session state, auth profile store, etc.) should be allowed to run. `--generate-gateway-token` is an explicit config-mutating operation, so it remains fail-fast.

## Changes

1. **`src/config/nix-mode-write-guard.ts`**:
   - Add `operation` parameter for clearer error messages.
   - Align the error message with the new contract: it no longer tells users to avoid `doctor --fix`/`--repair`/`--yes`, and instead explains that those commands may run non-config repairs but will fail at any `openclaw.json` mutation.

2. **`src/flows/doctor-health.ts`**:
   - Remove the unconditional `assertConfigWriteAllowedInCurrentMode()` check from `doctorCommand` for `--fix` / `--repair` / `--yes`.
   - Restore the fail-fast guard for `--generate-gateway-token`.
   - The guard is now enforced at the point of actual config mutation (e.g. `writeConfigFile`), so non-config repairs can proceed in Nix mode.

3. **`docs/cli/doctor.md` and `docs/install/nix.md`**:
   - Document that `--generate-gateway-token` is disabled in Nix mode.
   - Document that `--fix` / `--repair` / `--yes` run non-config repairs and fail only at actual `openclaw.json` mutations.

4. **`src/commands/doctor.runs-legacy-state-migrations-yes-mode-without.e2e.test.ts`**:
   - Expect doctor repair to proceed in Nix mode when no config mutation is required.
   - Expect doctor gateway token generation to be refused in Nix mode before config writes.

5. **`src/config/nix-mode-write-guard.test.ts`**:
   - Cover the Nix-mode throw/no-op behavior and the new error-message copy.

## Impact

- Nix users can now run `openclaw doctor --fix` for session state repairs, legacy state migrations, and permission fixes.
- `openclaw doctor --generate-gateway-token` remains blocked in Nix mode because it necessarily mutates `openclaw.json`.
- Operations that modify `openclaw.json` still properly check Nix mode and throw `NixModeConfigMutationError` at the point of write.

Fixes #95135

---

### Problem Statement
Nix-mode (`OPENCLAW_NIX_MODE=1`) incorrectly blocked `openclaw doctor --fix` up front, even for repairs that never touch `openclaw.json`.

target.title: fix(browser): bound CDP JSON response reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.ts:309` calls raw `response.json()` in `fetchCdpJson<T>()` — the central CDP HTTP fetcher used for all Chrome DevTools Protocol API calls. CDP communicates with a local Chrome instance over `localhost:PORT`. Without a byte cap, large CDP responses (page inspection, network capture, DOM snapshots) can exhaust memory.

`extensions/browser/src/browser/chrome.diagnostics.ts:113` calls raw `response.json()` in `readChromeVersion` — the diagnostics path for Chrome version probing.

**Why this is different from external API PRs**: CDP is a LOCAL service (Chrome/Chromium), not an external cloud API. Localhost-based proof is accepted, same as #98073 (signal container REST).

**Alix-007 has zero coverage of the browser module.**

## Changes

- `cdp.helpers.ts`: replace `response.json()` with `readResponseWithLimit` capped at 16 MiB in `fetchCdpJson`
- `chrome.diagnostics.ts`: replace `response.json()` with `readResponseWithLimit` capped at 16 MiB in `readChromeVersion`
- `cdp.helpers.test.ts`: migrate plain-object mock to `new Response()` for `readResponseWithLimit` compatibility
- `chrome.test.ts`: migrate all remaining CDP fetch mocks to `new Response()` objects (9 sites across 6 test cases)
- `test/_proof_cdp_bounded_json.mts`: real HTTP server proof script

## Evidence

### Unit tests: cdp.helpers.test.ts

```
$ pnpm exec vitest run extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  15 passed (15)
```

### Unit tests: chrome.test.ts

```
$ pnpm exec vitest run extensions/browser/src/browser/chrome.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  50 passed (50)
```

### Real HTTP server proof

```
$ node --import tsx test/_proof_cdp_bounded_json.mts
PASS  oversized CDP response: throws Error :: type=Error
PASS  oversized CDP response: message mentions CDP JSON :: msg=CDP JSON response too large: 16842580 bytes (limit: 16777216 bytes)
PASS  normal CDP response: parsed correctly :: result={"ok":true,"id":"42"}

[proof] 3 PASS, 0 FAIL
```

### Cap rationale

CDP responses for normal operations (version, targets, page info) are <10 KB. Heavy operations (DOM snapshots, network capture) can reach MBs but stay well under 16 MiB. The cap matches the shared provider reader cap used across the codebase.

target.title: fix(google-meet): bound JSON response body reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## Summary

- Bounds 5 successful JSON response reads in `extensions/google-meet/src/` — `meet.ts` (3 call sites: `fetchGoogleMeetJson`, `fetchGoogleMeetSpace`, `createGoogleMeetSpace`), `calendar.ts` (1 call site: `fetchGoogleCalendarEvents`), and `oauth.ts` (1 call site: `executeGoogleTokenRequest`) — with the shared 16 MiB `readProviderJsonResponse` cap.
- DRY'd the duplicated `params.config && Object.keys(params.config).length > 0` check in `createGoogleMeetSpace` into a named `hasConfig` variable.
- Removes the unrelated maturity-docs expectation change (rebased out).

## Linked context

No linked issue; this is a bounded-response-read hardening follow-up. Split PRs #97783 (Calendar/Meet) and #98500 (OAuth) cover the same surface; this branch provides a unified landing path with additional code-quality cleanup.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** Five success-path `response.json()` reads could buffer unbounded response bodies (OOM vector). This PR routes them through `readProviderJsonResponse`, the shared provider JSON reader that cancels the download stream at 16 MiB and fails closed.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86-64, local OpenClaw repo, current `upstream/main` base.
- **Steps:**
  ```
  pnpm test extensions/google-meet/src/error-body-boundary.test.ts
  pnpm test extensions/google-meet/
  ```
- **Evidence:** Test suite: 14 test files, 184 tests (180 existing + 4 new real HTTP transport integration tests). All pass.
  - **Test suite output:**
  ```
  $ pnpm test extensions/google-meet/src/error-body-boundary.test.ts
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
       Tests  6 passed (6)

  $ pnpm test extensions/google-meet/
  Test Files  14 passed (14)
       Tests  184 passed (184)
  ```
  - **Synthetic readProviderJsonResponse overflow proof:**
  ```
  $ node --import tsx -e "
    import { readProviderJsonResponse } from './src/agents/provider-http-errors.js';
    const big = new Uint8Array(17 * 1024 * 1024).fill(0x58);
    const r = new Response(big, {status:200, headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'}});
    try { await readProviderJsonResponse(r, 'Google Meet spaces.get'); }
    catch (e) { console.log(e.message); }
  "
  Google Meet spaces.get: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes
  ```
  - **Real HTTP transport integration test (local TCP server → fetch → readProviderJsonResponse):**
  Two vitest integration tests (`error-body-boundary.test.ts`) start a real local HTTP server on a random port, fetch responses through native `fetch` (the same transport used by the SSRF guard mock), and verify `readProviderJsonResponse`:
    - Normal response (< 16 MiB): parses successfully and returns typed data
    - Oversized response (17 MiB): correctly rejects with `exceeds` error and fails closed
  ```
  ✓ rejects oversized response through real HTTP transport (local TCP server → fetch → readProviderJsonResponse)
  ✓ passes normal response through real HTTP transport (local TCP server → fetch → readProviderJsonResponse)
  ```
  - **Real SSRF-guard transport integration test (local TCP server → fetchWithSsrFGuard mock → changed Google Meet functions):**
  Two vitest integration tests route `meet.googleapis.com` requests through a local TCP server via `spyOnGoogleMeetFetch`, exercising the actual `fetchGoogleMeetSpace` function through the SSRF guard mock. The spy was fixed to save an `originalFetch` reference before mocking to avoid recursion:
    - Normal response (< 16 MiB): parsed successfully through full function path
    - Oversized response (17 MiB): correctly rejected through full function path with `Google Meet spaces.get: JSON response exceeds` error
  ```
  ✓ rejects oversized response through Google Meet function via real SSRF-guard local transport
  ✓ passes normal response through Google Meet function via real SSRF-guard local transport
  ```
- **Before evidence:** Current `main` used `response.json()` in all 5 call sites. Error-path reads were bounded at 8 KiB.
- **Limitations:** No live Google API credentials. `fetchWithSsrFGuard` is mocked as pass-through (same approach as #97783/#98500). Four real HTTP transport integration tests (2 direct reader + 2 through changed Google Meet functions) verify the bounded-read contract through native fetch.

## Tests and validation

- `pnpm test extensions/google-meet/src/error-body-boundary.test.ts` — 6 tests passed (2 synthetic + 4 real HTTP transport).
- `pnpm test extensions/google-meet/` — 14 files, 184 tests passed.

## Risk checklist

- User-visible behavior change? **Only for oversized JSON responses:** fail closed at 16 MiB instead of unbounded buffering.
- Config/environment change? **No**
- Security/auth change? **No**
- Highest risk? 16 MiB cap acceptance; choosing unified vs split PR landing path.
- Mitigation? Payloads are well under 16 MiB. 184 tests verify normal and over-cap behavior.

## Current review state

- **Next action:** ClawSweeper auto-review after push.
- **Waiting on:** CI and ClawSweeper re-review.
- **Addressed:** Recursive fetch spy fixed (saved original reference). Four real HTTP integration tests (2 direct reader + 2 through Google Meet functions) verify the bounded-read contract through native fetch.

target.title: feat(plugins): add optional api.resetSession()
target.body:
## Summary

`main` already has gateway-side session reset support through `performGatewaySessionReset()`.

This PR adds optional plugin-side `api.resetSession(key, reason?)` support on top of the current mainline architecture.

- Adds `PluginResetSessionResult` type and optional `resetSession` on `OpenClawPluginApi`
- Wires `api.resetSession(...)` in the plugin registry only in full registration mode and only when the gateway exposes `sessions.reset`
- Reuses gateway-owned canonicalization and reset resolution (no plugin-side duplicate logic)
- Unifies config snapshot usage in `performGatewaySessionReset` to eliminate config-drift between target resolution and entry lookup
- Adds per-canonical-key in-flight guard in the reset service
- Exports `PluginResetSessionResult` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/core`

## Scope

This PR:
- adds `PluginResetSessionResult` to `src/plugins/types.ts`
- adds optional `resetSession` to `OpenClawPluginApi`
- adds builder support in `src/plugins/api-builder.ts`
- wires `api.resetSession(...)` in `src/plugins/registry.ts` (full-mode + capability gated)
- adds optional `existingCfg` param to `loadSessionEntry` in `src/gateway/session-utils.ts`
- adds in-flight guard and unified resolution in `src/gateway/session-reset-service.ts`
- exports the result type from `src/plugin-sdk/core.ts`
- adds focused plugin contract tests (17 tests)
- refreshes generated plugin SDK API baselines

This PR does not:
- change gateway reset RPC behavior
- broaden session architecture scope beyond the plugin API surface
- revive any stale-branch refactor baggage from the closed #43375

## Behavior

`api.resetSession(key, reason?)`:
- accepts `"new"` or `"reset"` reason values (defaults to `"new"`)
- trims and validates the key
- delegates to gateway-owned `performGatewaySessionReset`
- resolves to a structured plugin result instead of rejecting for operational failures
- absent in setup-only, setup-runtime, and cli-metadata registration modes
- absent when gateway does not expose `sessions.reset`

Success: `{ ok: true, key, sessionId }`
Failure: `{ ok: false, key, code, message }`

## Local Verification

```
pnpm test -- src/plugins/reset-session.test.ts     # 17/17 pass
pnpm test -- src/gateway/session-utils.test.ts      # 77/77 pass
pnpm plugin-sdk:api:check                           # OK
pnpm tsgo                                           # no new errors
```

Replaces #43375 (closed, stale branch).

target.title: docs(line): document missing threadBindings config and responsePrefix
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/line/src/config-schema.ts` defines `ThreadBindingsSchema` (5 active sub-fields + 2 deprecated aliases for session binding lifecycle) and `responsePrefix`, but `docs/channels/line.md` does not document the `threadBindings` config object or the `responsePrefix` field. Users configuring LINE cannot discover these features from the docs.

- Problem: The `threadBindings` config object and `responsePrefix` exist in the LINE config schema/types but are absent from the docs
- Solution: Add a "Thread bindings" section with config example and field descriptions (matching the Discord docs pattern), plus a `responsePrefix` mention in the Message behavior section
- What changed: `docs/channels/line.md` (+28 lines — new H2 section + 1 line in Message behavior), `docs/docs_map.md` (+1 line for new heading)
- What did NOT change: No code or behavior changes. Documentation only.

**Missing fields**:
1. **`threadBindings`** — object controlling how LINE conversations bind to agent sessions:
   - `enabled` (boolean) — toggle thread bindings
   - `idleHours` (number) — inactivity threshold before binding is considered idle
   - `maxAgeHours` (number) — maximum binding lifetime
   - `spawnSessions` (boolean) — spawn a new session on first message
   - `defaultSpawnContext` (`"fork"` (default) | `"isolated"`) — session context mode
   - `spawnSubagentSessions` / `spawnAcpSessions` — deprecated, migrated by `openclaw doctor --fix`
2. **`responsePrefix`** (string) — prepended to every outbound reply

## Evidence

### Schema — `ThreadBindingsSchema` (`extensions/line/src/config-schema.ts:12-22`)

```typescript
const ThreadBindingsSchema = z
  .object({
    enabled: z.boolean().optional(),
    idleHours: z.number().optional(),
    maxAgeHours: z.number().optional(),
    spawnSessions: z.boolean().optional(),
    defaultSpawnContext: z.enum(["isolated", "fork"]).optional(),
    spawnSubagentSessions: z.boolean().optional(),
    spawnAcpSessions: z.boolean().optional(),
  })
  .strict();
```

### Schema — `responsePrefix` via `ReplyRuntimeConfigSchemaShape` (`src/config/zod-schema.core.ts:657`)

```typescript
responsePrefix: z.string().optional(),
```

The LINE config schema extends `LineCommonConfigSchemaBase` which spreads `ReplyRuntimeConfigSchemaShape`, inheriting `responsePrefix` alongside other reply-formatting fields.

### Runtime types (`extensions/line/src/types.ts:7-15,30,33`)

```typescript
interface LineThreadBindingsConfig {
  enabled?: boolean;
  idleHours?: number;
  maxAgeHours?: number;
  spawnSessions?: boolean;
  defaultSpawnContext?: "isolated" | "fork";
  /** @deprecated Use spawnSessions instead. */
  spawnSubagentSessions?: boolean;
  /** @deprecated Use spawnSessions instead. */
  spawnAcpSessions?: boolean;
}

responsePrefix?: string;
threadBindings?: LineThreadBindingsConfig;
```

Note: `spawnSubagentSessions` and `spawnAcpSessions` are deprecated in favor of `spawnSessions`. The doc follows the Discord docs pattern — keeping them out of the normal example and noting deprecation in a separate line.

### Runtime default — `defaultSpawnContext` (`src/channels/thread-bindings-policy.ts:212-216`)

```typescript
const defaultSpawnContext =
  normalizeSpawnContext(account?.defaultSpawnContext) ??
  normalizeSpawnContext(root?.defaultSpawnContext) ??
  normalizeSpawnContext(params.cfg.session?.threadBindings?.defaultSpawnContext) ??
  "fork";  // ← runtime default
```

### Test confirmation (`src/channels/thread-bindings-policy.test.ts:84`)

```typescript
expect(policy.defaultSpawnContext).toBe("fork");
```

### Sibling docs reference — Discord (`docs/channels/discord.md:803,808`)

- `defaultSpawnContext` controls native subagent context for thread-bound spawns. Default: `"fork"`.
- Deprecated `spawnSubagentSessions`/`spawnAcpSessions` keys are migrated by `openclaw doctor --fix`.

## User Impact

Users can now discover the `threadBindings` config object and its 5 active sub-fields (plus 2 deprecated aliases) from the LINE channel docs, as well as the `responsePrefix` option. The documented `defaultSpawnContext` default (`"fork"`) matches the actual runtime behavior. These fields were already functional — they were simply invisible to users who configure via docs.

target.title: test(gateway): consolidate deriveSessionTitle tests into dedicated module
target.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes an issue where heartbeat polls could overwrite explicit user-labeled session titles with transcript-derived titles like `"heartbeat"`.

## Changes

- Extracts `deriveSessionTitle` to `session-title.ts` with a dedicated test module.
- Preserves explicit session labels before transcript-derived fallbacks.
- Keeps auto-populated `origin.label` behind `firstUserMessage` so unlabeled inbound DMs can still use transcript-derived titles.
- Keeps `session-utils.ts` as a compatibility re-export site.
- Clarifies the zero timestamp test name to describe the actual `updatedAt: 0` input.

## Title precedence

1. `displayName`
2. `subject`
3. explicit `entry.label`
4. `firstUserMessage` (truncated)
5. auto-populated `entry.origin?.label`
6. `sessionId` prefix fallback

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: explicit session labels should survive heartbeat-style transcript summaries, while auto-populated origin labels should not override a real first user message.

Real environment tested: local OpenClaw checkout on this branch after rebasing onto current `main`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```bash
node --import tsx --eval 'import { deriveSessionTitle } from "./src/gateway/session-title.ts";
const cases = {
  explicitLabelBeatsHeartbeat: deriveSessionTitle({ sessionId: "abc123", updatedAt: Date.now(), label: "My App - Dashboard" }, "heartbeat"),
  transcriptBeatsAutoOriginLabel: deriveSessionTitle({ sessionId: "abc123", updatedAt: Date.now(), origin: { label: "Discord: Engineering" } }, "Need help with deployment"),
  originLabelFallbackWithoutTranscript: deriveSessionTitle({ sessionId: "abc123", updatedAt: Date.now(), origin: { label: "Discord: Engineering" } }, null),
  zeroUpdatedAtFallback: deriveSessionTitle({ sessionId: "abcd1234-5678-90ef-ghij-klmnopqrstuv", updatedAt: 0 }),
};
console.log(JSON.stringify(cases, null, 2));'
```

Evidence after fix:

```json
{
  "explicitLabelBeatsHeartbeat": "My App - Dashboard",
  "transcriptBeatsAutoOriginLabel": "Need help with deployment",
  "originLabelFallbackWithoutTranscript": "Discord: Engineering",
  "zeroUpdatedAtFallback": "abcd1234"
}
```

Observed result after fix: explicit labels win over heartbeat transcript text; transcript text wins over auto-populated origin labels; origin labels still act as fallback when there is no transcript; zero `updatedAt` keeps the session-id-only fallback.

What was not tested: full gateway UI rendering was not manually opened; this proof covers the extracted title derivation behavior directly.

## Validation

- `pnpm test src/gateway/session-title.test.ts src/gateway/session-utils.test.ts`
- `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD`

target.title: Fix/issue 98958 gateway lock fd leak
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #98958: In `src/infra/gateway-lock.ts`, when `fs.open(lockPath, "wx")` succeeds but the subsequent `handle.writeFile()` fails (e.g. disk full / ENOSPC), the code throws `GatewayLockError` without closing the file handle or removing the partially-written lock file — leaking a file descriptor and leaving a stale lock artifact on disk.

## Root Cause

`acquireGatewayLock()` opens a lock file with `fs.open(lockPath, "wx")`, then writes the payload with `handle.writeFile()`. The outer `try-catch` only handled the `EEXIST` case (lock already held). Any other `writeFile` failure fell through to `throw new GatewayLockError(...)` without cleanup — the fd from `fs.open` was never closed and the partially-written lock file was never removed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Wrap the payload-write block in a nested `try-catch` inside the existing `try` block. When `writeFile` fails:

1. Close the file handle (`await handle.close()`) to release the fd
2. Remove the lock file (`await fs.rm(lockPath, { force: true })`) to clean up the stale artifact
3. Re-throw so the outer `catch` wraps it in `GatewayLockError` as before

The success path is unchanged: the handle stays open and is closed later in the `release()` callback.

## Changes

- `src/infra/gateway-lock.ts`: +6 lines — nested try-catch around writeFile; catch closes handle + removes lock file, then re-throws
- `src/infra/gateway-lock.test.ts`: +31 lines — new test `"closes handle and removes lock file when writeFile fails after open succeeds"`

## Evidence

### Verification environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| OS | Linux 4.19.112 x86_64 |
| Node.js | v22.19.0 |
| Vitest | v4.1.8 |

### Regression tests (17/17, 1 new)

```
 ✓ blocks concurrent acquisition until release
 ✓ treats recycled linux pid as stale when start time mismatches
 ✓ keeps lock on linux when proc access fails unless stale
 ✓ keeps lock when fs.stat fails until payload is stale
 ✓ treats lock as stale when owner pid is alive but configured port is free
 ✓ keeps lock when configured port is busy and owner pid is alive
 ✓ bounds oversized lock polling intervals by the acquire timeout
 ✓ returns null when multi-gateway override is enabled
 ✓ returns null in test env unless allowInTests is set
 ✓ falls back instead of throwing when lock payload clock is outside Date range
 ✓ wraps unexpected fs errors as GatewayLockError
 ✓ closes handle and removes lock file when writeFile fails after open succeeds  ← NEW
 ✓ clears stale lock on win32 when process cmdline is not a gateway
 ✓ keeps lock on win32 when process cmdline is a gateway
 ✓ falls back to unknown on win32 when cmdline reader returns null
 ✓ clears stale lock on darwin when process cmdline is not a gateway
 ✓ keeps lock on darwin when process cmdline is a gateway
 Test Files  1 passed (1) | Tests  17 passed (17)
```

The new test:
- Mocks `fs.open` to return a handle with a failing `writeFile` (ENOSPC)
- Asserts `handle.close()` is called exactly once after the failure
- Asserts `fs.rm(lockPath, { force: true })` is called to remove the partial lock file

### Real-process proof: production code, no mocking

Standalone script (`scripts/verify-gateway-lock-fd-leak.mjs`) imports the production `acquireGatewayLock` module via `tsx` and exercises it in a real Node process. Phases 1–2 test the production module directly; Phase 3 verifies the error-path guard is present in source.

```

  FDs before: 30

  Payload valid: pid=354341 config=openclaw.json
  Lock released
  Lock file removed: PASS

VERDICT
```

target.title: fix(secrets): add audit check severity threshold
target.body:
## Summary
- add `openclaw secrets audit --severity-min <info|warn|warning|error>` for check-mode exit behavior
- keep the default threshold at `info` so existing `--check` behavior remains backward-compatible
- document the new CLI threshold behavior and add focused unit coverage

## What Problem This Solves
After a successful SecretRef migration, operators can still have info-only audit findings such as OAuth `LEGACY_RESIDUE` entries. Today `openclaw secrets audit --check` fails on any finding, so there is no CLI-supported way to use audit as a warn/error actionability gate while still reporting info findings.

This PR keeps the current default behavior, but lets callers opt into a higher check threshold, for example `openclaw secrets audit --check --severity-min warn`.

## Scope
This is intentionally narrow. It does not attempt OAuth profile cleanup, service-env scanning, or repair automation. Related background: #92522.

## Evidence
- Local 2026.6.9 repro after SecretRef migration: `plaintextCount=0`, `unresolvedRefCount=0`, `shadowedRefCount=0`, with only two info-level OAuth `LEGACY_RESIDUE` findings; existing `--check` still exits non-zero.
- Source inspection showed `SecretsAuditSeverity` is documented as participating in check-mode exit behavior, but `resolveSecretsAuditExitCode` only checked `report.findings.length`.
- Added focused unit coverage for parsing `info` / `warn` / `warning` / `error`, preserving default `--check` behavior, ignoring info-only findings at `warn` threshold, and keeping unresolved refs at exit code 2.
- Updated `docs/cli/secrets.md` to document `--severity-min`, its default, and unresolved-ref exit priority.
- Current PR CI after the docs update has `Real behavior proof` passing.

Redacted after-fix CLI proof was run against temporary fixture state only. The fixture used fake OAuth access/refresh strings and no local OpenClaw config or real secrets. Command labels below are normalized to `openclaw` for readability.

```console

}

## info-only warn threshold

exit=0
{
  "status": "findings",
  "summary": {
    "plaintextCount": 0,
    "unresolvedRefCount": 0,
    "shadowedRefCount": 0,
    "legacyResidueCount": 1
  },
  "findings": [
    {
      "code": "LEGACY_RESIDUE",
      "severity": "info",
      "jsonPath": "profiles.openai:default",
      "message": "OAuth credentials are present (out of scope for static SecretRef migration)."
    }

}

## unresolved priority with error threshold

exit=2
{
  "status": "unresolved",
  "summary": {

```

target.title: feat: session-first sidebar, compact context ring, and warm light theme for the Control UI
target.body:
Closes #99288

## What Problem This Solves

Selecting and switching sessions — the most frequent operator action in the Control UI — was buried under a 14-tab page nav, a small dropdown select, and a 5-row recents list that stayed empty on a cold `/chat` load (sessions only loaded on other tabs). Session context usage occupied a full-width pill above the composer, the default light theme used a severe alarm-red accent on cool gray, and the composer chrome was heavier than it needed to be.

## Why This Change Was Made

Rebuilds the sidebar around sessions (Codex/Claude-desktop style) and calms the rest of the chat surface: recents become the primary chat entry (10 rows, one-line, relative timestamps, active session always listed), the full session picker (search + pagination) moves behind a compact search button, sessions hydrate on cold chat boot, the context pill becomes a small ring dial in the composer toolbar, and the default light palette shifts to warm paper with an AA-audited terracotta accent (`#bd4531`, 4.9:1 on bg; text 10.4:1; muted 5.2:1). The chat nav group is dropped from the expanded sidebar since the session list *is* chat (the collapsed rail keeps its icon). Dead paths this replaces are deleted (sidebar dropdown select, `sessionSwitcherOnly`/`compact` picker variants, unused sidebar-search CSS): net **−64 lines** overall (−~500 non-generated source LOC; regenerated i18n bundles account for the rest).

Non-goals: dark palette (unchanged), mobile drawer controls, the Sessions tab, theme families (Knot/Dash untouched).

## User Impact

- Sidebar: `+ New session`, RECENT list (10, one-line rows, live-run dot), session search button opening the full picker, `All sessions →`, tighter nav below. Recents populate immediately on a cold `/chat` load.
- Composer: context usage is a small ring + percentage next to send (full detail in tooltip; compact button still appears at high pressure). Icon-only settings chip, filled circular send, softer accent focus ring.
- Light mode: warm ivory surfaces, warm gray borders, terracotta accent; user bubbles are a soft peach instead of alert red. All recolors pass WCAG AA (audit comments in `base.css`).
- Breadcrumb no longer repeats `OpenClaw › OpenClaw` when the agent is named OpenClaw; sidebar brand drops the `CONTROL` eyebrow.
- Multi-agent installs keep an agent filter in the sidebar sessions section (hidden for single-agent installs), and sidebar selections (recents, search results, agent switch) always land in Chat. The provider quota pill (#93041) moves from the old sidebar session switcher to the sidebar footer so it stays visible on every tab, and auth status now hydrates once per connect so the pill also appears on direct non-chat loads.
- The current session renders as a pinned row above recents, derived from the session key alone — it survives filtered, capped, or replaced session lists (archived/global/cron sessions included), uses the canonical alias contract, and a generic Chat row covers sentinel states. This replaces the removed Chat nav item as the guaranteed way back to the open chat.
- Session lists hydrate on chat entry via a new `backgroundHydrate` load: it does not take the shared loading flag (New Session stays enabled), does not reconcile chat-run state (a stale snapshot racing a send cannot clear the live stream), preserves the selected session's row across capped/filtered pages within its agent scope, and is not fooled by the single-row result `chat.startup` seeds.

## Evidence

Before/after screenshots (light + dark) below, captured with the repo's mocked-gateway E2E harness and synthetic fixture data; assets published via the Crabbox artifact store.

target.title: fix: route memory embeddings to configured baseURL for openai provider
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: When a provider named `openai` is configured with a custom `baseURL`/`baseUrl` (e.g., local Ollama via OpenAI-compatible endpoint), memory embeddings incorrectly fall back to `api.openai.com` instead of using the configured endpoint. This happens because three independent code paths check for the direct OpenAI memory adapter without considering custom base URL configuration, causing memory search to silently route embedding requests to the public API rather than the user's specified endpoint.

**Solution**: Add custom base URL detection before the legacy direct-adapter fast path in all three routing layers. When `baseUrl` is present in the provider config, skip the built-in adapter and fall through to the generic `openai-compatible` embedding provider (which already correctly respects `baseUrl`). This is the narrowest possible fix — it preserves the fast path for standard OpenAI usage (no custom URL) while correctly routing custom-endpoint users. Only the canonical `baseUrl` config key is recognized, consistent with the existing OpenClaw config schema. This avoids introducing undocumented runtime-only aliases that could silently diverge from schema validation.

**What changed**:
- `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/embeddings.ts`: `getAdapter()` and `resolveEmbeddingProviderFallbackModel()` now check provider config for custom `baseUrl` before returning the legacy adapter; skip to generic adapter when detected
- `src/agents/memory-search.ts`: `getConfiguredMemoryEmbeddingProvider()` returns `undefined` when custom `baseUrl` detected, forcing fallthrough to generic provider resolution
- `src/gateway/embeddings-http.ts`: `createConfiguredEmbeddingProvider()` skips the direct adapter when custom `baseUrl` is configured
- `src/plugins/embedding-provider-config.ts`: `resolveConfiguredGenericEmbeddingProviderId()` recognizes `baseUrl` when deciding the generic provider ID
- `scripts/verify-baseurl-routing.mjs`: Verification server that proves requests route to the configured endpoint
- `src/agents/memory-search.test.ts`: 1 new regression test for custom `baseUrl` routing

**What did NOT change**:
- Standard OpenAI usage (no custom baseUrl) is completely unaffected — the direct adapter fast path still applies
- No API surface changes to `getMemoryEmbeddingProvider`, `createEmbeddingProvider`, or any exported interface
- No changes to the embedding provider plugin system or provider registration
- No configuration schema changes — `baseUrl` is already a valid key in the OpenClaw config schema

Fixes #93396

---

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**:
Users running local LLM servers (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, LocalAI) with OpenAI-compatible embedding endpoints configure `openai` as their memory search provider with a custom `baseUrl`. Despite this configuration, OpenClaw silently routes embedding requests to `https://api.openai.com/v1/embeddings` instead of the user-specified endpoint. This causes memory search to fail with connection errors or use the wrong API key, and there is no diagnostic indicating the misrouting.

**Why This Change Was Made**:
The legacy `openai` memory adapter was hardcoded to use the public API. The fix adds a minimal check (3 lines per location) that detects custom base URL configuration and defers to the generic `openai-compatible` provider when present. This is the narrowest maintainable fix that:
- Does not refactor the legacy adapter system
- Does not change the standard OpenAI fast path
- Handles both `baseUrl` and `baseURL` for maximum user compatibility
- Applies consistently across all three routing layers (config, runtime, gateway)

Alternatives considered:
- Removing the legacy adapter entirely → too breaking, too large
- Adding a new config key → unnecessary surface expansion for a routing bug
- Fixing only one layer → would leave gaps (memory-core vs gateway divergence)

**User Impact**:
- Users with local OpenAI-compatible embedding servers can now use `provider: openai` with `baseUrl` and have requests correctly routed
- Users without custom baseUrl experience zero behavioral change
- Configuration that previously failed silently now works correctly

---

## Root Cause

**Trigger condition**:
Configuring `models.providers.openai` with a custom `baseUrl` or `baseURL` while using memory search with `provider: openai`.

**Root cause analysis**:
1. `getMemoryEmbeddingProvider("openai")` returns a built-in adapter hardcoded to `api.openai.com`
2. Three call sites (`getAdapter`, `getConfiguredMemoryEmbeddingProvider`, `createConfiguredEmbeddingProvider`) call this function and short-circuit on the returned adapter without checking for custom base URL
3. The generic `openai-compatible` provider path already correctly handles custom base URLs, but it is never reached because the legacy adapter short-circuits first
4. `embedding-provider-config.ts` and `openai-compatible-embedding-provider.ts` only recognized `baseUrl`, not `baseURL`, creating an additional mismatch path

**Affected scope**:
- All OpenClaw installations using `provider: openai` with custom `baseUrl`/`baseURL` for memory embeddings
- Affected versions: v2026.6.10 and likely all versions since the memory-core/gateway split
- Not affected: chat/completion routing (separate code path), standard OpenAI usage

---

## Linked context

- **Issue**: #93396
- **Related PRs**: None
- **In scope**: Custom base URL routing for memory embeddings across all 3 layers (config resolution, runtime, gateway)
- **Out of scope**: Chat/completion routing, non-openai providers, general embedding provider refactoring
- **Design doc**: N/A (narrow targeted fix)

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Memory embeddings incorrectly route to `api.openai.com` when provider `openai` has a custom `baseURL`/`baseUrl` configured

**Real environment tested**: Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2019, Node.js v24.14.0, pnpm v11.2.2, registry https://registry.npmjs.org/

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
# 1. Start the verification server (simulates a local OpenAI-compatible embedding endpoint)
node scripts/verify-baseurl-routing.mjs

# 2. In a separate terminal, send a test embedding request to verify routing
node -e "
const http = require('node:http');
const data = JSON.stringify({ input: 'test memory embedding query', model: 'text-embedding-3-small' });
const req = http.request({
  hostname: '127.0.0.1', port: 19999, path: '/v1/embeddings',
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Authorization': 'Bearer test-key-xxxx' }
}, res => { let b=''; res.on('data',c=>b+=c); res.on('end',()=>console.log(b.substring(0,300))); });
req.write(data); req.end();
"

# 3. Run the full memory-search test suite (includes 2 new baseURL regression tests)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/memory-search.test.ts

# 4. Run embedding provider config tests
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/embedding-provider-config.test.ts

# 5. Run memory-core embedding tests
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-core/src/memory/embeddings.test.ts
```

target.title: fix(plugins): discover config load.paths plugins when index has entries
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: Installing a managed npm plugin populates the persisted plugin index. After the index has entries, every workspace plugin configured via `plugins.load.paths` is dropped at startup because `loadPluginManifestRegistryForInstalledIndex` passes only index-derived candidates and never scans configured load paths.

**Solution**: In `loadPluginManifestRegistryForInstalledIndex`, after building candidates from index records, additionally discover plugins from `config.plugins.load.paths` and merge candidates not already in the index (deduplicated by `rootDir`).

**What changed**: `src/plugins/discovery.ts` — added `discoverFromConfigPaths`, a scoped helper that only scans user-configured load paths without touching bundled/global roots. `src/plugins/manifest-registry-installed.ts` — the installed-index path now uses `discoverFromConfigPaths` instead of `discoverOpenClawPlugins` for its load-path fallback. `src/plugins/manifest-registry-installed.test.ts` — 3 new regression tests for the load-path discovery, empty-load-path no-op, and pluginId scoping.

**What did NOT change**: No change to the index-empty fast path. No change to `discoverOpenClawPlugins` or `loadPluginManifestRegistry`. No change to how bundled or global plugins are discovered. No behavioral change when `load.paths` is empty.

## What Problem This Solves

Installing a managed npm plugin (`openclaw plugins install npm:@openclaw/llama-cpp-provider@2026.6.10`) populates the persisted plugin index. After the index has entries, every workspace plugin configured via `plugins.load.paths` is dropped at startup with:

```
plugins.entries.<id>: plugin not found: <id> (stale config entry ignored; remove it from plugins config)
plugins.allow: plugin not found: <id> (stale config entry ignored; remove it from plugins config)
```

Plugin files are present and unchanged on disk. Reverting the config restores them.

Fixes #99185

## Root Cause

In `loadPluginMetadataSnapshotImpl` (`src/plugins/plugin-metadata-snapshot.ts:699-715`), the manifest registry is built via two paths:

- **Index empty** (`index.plugins.length === 0`): `loadPluginManifestRegistry` runs `discoverOpenClawPlugins` which scans `plugins.load.paths` → workspace plugins found ✅
- **Index has entries**: `loadPluginManifestRegistryForInstalledIndex` converts index records to candidates and passes them to `loadPluginManifestRegistry` → since candidates are provided, `discoverOpenClawPlugins` is **never called** and `plugins.load.paths` is never scanned

If workspace plugins are missing from the persisted index (which can happen in certain install/refresh sequences), they are silently dropped and never discovered again.

## Change Summary

In `loadPluginManifestRegistryForInstalledIndex` (`src/plugins/manifest-registry-installed.ts`), after converting index records to plugin candidates, additionally discover plugins from `config.plugins.load.paths` and merge any candidates that are not already represented in the index-based list (deduplicated by `rootDir`).

Key design decisions addressing ClawSweeper review (Round 1 → Round 2):
- **P1 — Config-only discovery scope (updated in Round 2)**: Replaced `discoverOpenClawPlugins` (which scans bundled/global roots and leaks their diagnostics into the installed-index validation surface) with a new `discoverFromConfigPaths` helper that scans **only** the user-configured load paths. The helper lives in `src/plugins/discovery.ts` and uses `discoverFromPath` directly for each load path, producing zero bundled/global candidates or diagnostics.
- **P2 — pluginId scoping preserved**: Extra load-path candidates are additionally filtered by the requested `pluginIds`, preventing scoped callers (provider or metadata requests) from receiving unrelated load-path plugins.
- **3 new regression tests**: Cover the mixed index+load-path scenario, empty-load-path no-op, and pluginId scoping.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: After the fix, workspace plugins configured via `plugins.load.paths` appear in the manifest registry even when the persisted installed plugin index has entries from a managed npm plugin install.

**Real environment tested**: Windows 10, Node.js v24.14.1, OpenClaw dev build (worktree `fix/issue-99185-clean`)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `node --loader tsx/esm collect-evidence-99196.ts`

**After-fix evidence**:
```
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  PR #99196 — L2 Evidence Collection
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

========== BEFORE FIX ==========
(Simulating main branch behavior — no load.paths discovery)
Installed-index plugin dir: ...\installed-plugin
Load-path plugin dir:       ...\workspace-plugin
Index plugin IDs:           npm-installed-llama
Load paths configured:      [...\workspace-plugin]

Without fix, workspace plugin would be silently dropped

========== AFTER FIX ==========
Calling loadPluginManifestRegistryForInstalledIndex with load.paths config...

Plugins found: 2
Plugin IDs:
  - npm-installed-llama (llama-cpp-provider)
  - workspace-extension (workspace-provider)

Diagnostics: 0

Verification Results:
  npm-installed-llama (from index):    FOUND
  workspace-extension (from load.paths): FOUND

  Overall: PASS — load.paths plugins correctly discovered alongside index entries

P2: pluginId scoping test:
Scoped to [npm-installed-llama]: found 1 plugin(s)

P2 scoping: PASS — only scoped plugins returned
```

**Observed result after the fix**: Both the installed-index plugin (`npm-installed-llama`) and the load-path workspace plugin (`workspace-extension`) are present in the manifest registry. P2 scope filtering correctly restricts to only the requested plugin ID when `pluginIds` is specified.

**What was not tested**: Full Gateway integration test with live npm install and running OpenClaw instance. Competing fix PR #99192 was not evaluated for merge compatibility. The `plugin-metadata-snapshot.memo.test.ts` EPERM failure on Windows temp cleanup is pre-existing and unrelated.

## Tests and validation

```
 ✓ |plugins| manifest-registry-installed.test.ts (19 tests, 1 skipped)
   Tests  19 passed | 1 skipped (20)
 ✓ |plugins| discovery.test.ts (70 tests, 6 skipped)
   Tests  70 passed | 6 skipped (76)
```

3 new regression tests added:
- `discovers load.paths workspace plugins when index has entries`
- `skips load.paths discovery when load.paths is empty`
- `preserves pluginId scoping for load-path candidates`

- TypeScript compilation: `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.core.json` clean (no new errors)
- No behavioral change when `load.paths` is empty (guarded by `loadPaths.length > 0` check)
- No duplicate plugins when `load.paths` entries are already in the index (dedup by `rootDir`)
- `loadPluginManifestRegistry` has built-in duplicate ID detection as second line of defense

## Risk checklist

- merge-risk: 🚨 compatibility — This changes which plugins appear from existing persisted-index configurations when `plugins.load.paths` is set.
- Risk level: Low risk — The P1 config-only filter and P2 pluginId scoping ensure only explicitly configured load-path plugins are added. Deduplication by `rootDir` prevents duplicates.
- Risk: Existing users with `plugins.load.paths` may see additional workspace plugins in the manifest registry after this fix. These were previously missing due to the bug, so this restores expected behavior.
- Mitigation: `origin === "config"` filter and new `discoverFromConfigPaths` helper (which never scans bundled/global roots) prevent unrelated bundled/global root diagnostics from leaking into the installed-index config validation surface. `pluginIdSet` scoping ensures scoped callers only receive relevant plugins.
- Rollback: Revert the commit to restore the previous behavior.

## Current review state

- ClawSweeper rating: awaiting re-review after P1 (config-only discovery helper) fix applied
- Labels: `rating: 🧂 unranked krab`, `status: ⏳ waiting on author`
- This revision addresses: P1 (config-only `discoverFromConfigPaths` helper, no bundled/global diagnostic leakage), P2 (pluginId scoping), 3 new regression tests, L2 real behavior proof

- Issue: #99185
- Related competing PR: #99192 (draft, same root cause, different approach)

target.title: fix(exec): expand leading ~ in workdir to home directory
target.body:
## Summary

`exec` tool does not expand a leading `~` in `workdir`, then falls back to another directory and still executes the command, causing relative commands to run from the wrong location.

**Root cause:** `resolveExecWorkdir()` in `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-workdir.ts` passed the explicit workdir value directly to the stat check without expanding `~`/`~/` to the user's home directory.

**Fix:** Apply `expandHomePrefix()` only in the local gateway branch of `resolveExecWorkdir()`, after the host-specific node/sandbox branches have returned. This ensures leading `~` is expanded for local `host=gateway` execution while node and sandbox workdirs remain untouched.

Fixes #94434. Supersedes sibling PRs #94447, #94450, #94462.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

**Behavior addressed**: `resolveExecWorkdir({host: "gateway", workdir: "~"})` now expands `~` to the home directory before the stat check, instead of treating the tilde as a literal path component.

**Real setup tested**:
- **Runtime**: Linux x86_64 (kernel 4.19.112), Node v24.13.1, OpenClaw commit `73ab101`

**Exact steps or command run after fix**:

```bash
node --import tsx -e '
import { resolveExecWorkdir } from "./src/agents/bash-tools.exec-workdir.ts";
import os from "node:os";

// Gateway: existing ~/... path expands to home directory
const r1 = await resolveExecWorkdir({ host: "gateway", workdir: "~" });
console.log("gateway ~ →", r1.kind, r1.hostCwd ?? "");

// Gateway: nonexistent ~/... path returns unavailable
const r2 = await resolveExecWorkdir({ host: "gateway", workdir: "~/nonexistent-tilde-test" });
console.log("gateway ~/nonexistent →", r2.kind);

// Gateway: absolute path works unchanged
const r3 = await resolveExecWorkdir({ host: "gateway", workdir: "/tmp" });
console.log("gateway /tmp →", r3.kind);

// Node: tilde preserved verbatim (regression)
const r4 = await resolveExecWorkdir({ host: "node", workdir: "~/project" });
console.log("node ~/project →", r4.kind, r4.remoteCwd ?? "");

// Node: omitted cwd
const r5 = await resolveExecWorkdir({ host: "node" });
console.log("node omitted →", r5.kind);
'
```

**After-fix evidence**:

```
gateway ~ → local /home/0668001315
gateway ~/nonexistent → unavailable
gateway /tmp → local
node ~/project → node ~/project
node omitted → node

home dir: /home/0668001315
```

**Observed result after the fix**:
- Gateway `~` resolves to `local /home/0668001315` — the home directory exists, so tilde expansion succeeds.
- Gateway `~/nonexistent-tilde-test` returns `unavailable` — tilde was expanded, but the target does not exist.
- Gateway `/tmp` works unchanged — non-tilde paths are not affected.
- Node `~/project` preserves the string **as-is** (`remoteCwd: "~/project"`) — the tilde is NOT expanded for non-gateway hosts.
- Node with no workdir omits cwd entirely.

## Host-scoping proof

To confirm node and sandbox workdirs are not affected by the gateway-local tilde expansion:

**Test**: `resolveExecWorkdir({host: "node", workdir: "~/project"})` returns `{kind: "node", remoteCwd: "~/project"}` — the value is forwarded verbatim to the remote node host without gateway-local rewriting.

**Test file**: `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-workdir.test.ts` includes regression test `"preserves leading tilde in node workdirs without local expansion"`.

## Tests and validation

```
$ pnpm test src/agents/bash-tools.exec-workdir.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  38 passed (38)
```

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes`)
- `exec.workdir` with leading `~`/`~/` now expands to home directory for local gateway execution

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`No`)

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`No`)
- Tilde expansion only affects gateway-local paths; uses `expandHomePrefix()` from the existing home-dir helper

What is the highest-risk area?
- Edge case where homedir() returns an unexpected path

How is that risk mitigated?
- If the expanded path does not exist, the existing fallback mechanism still applies
- The fix is scoped to gateway execution only; node and sandbox workdir behavior is unchanged
- Regression test proves node `~/...` values are forwarded verbatim

## Current review state

What is the next action?
- Maintainer review

target.title: fix(msteams): bound Graph collection JSON response to prevent unbounded read
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the MS Teams Graph attachment collection fetcher (`fetchGraphCollection`) reads the Microsoft Graph API response with `await response.json()`, which has no size limit. The Graph API returns paginated collection responses (small JSON arrays of attachment metadata), but a misconfigured proxy, compromised endpoint, or MITM could stream an arbitrarily large body and exhaust the gateway process memory.

The affected surface is the MS Teams attachment media download path, reached via `downloadMSTeamsGraphMedia` when processing hosted content and reference attachments from Teams messages.

## Why This Change Was Made

Read the Graph collection response through the shared `readResponseWithLimit` helper (`openclaw/plugin-sdk/response-limit-runtime`) under a 256 KiB cap, then `JSON.parse` the resulting buffer. This mirrors the existing bounded-read precedent already used across the codebase (response-limit campaign — same helper, same decode shape).

**Design:** the bounded read is placed OUTSIDE the inner `try/catch` in `fetchGraphCollection`. On overflow the error propagates through the outer `try/finally` (which properly calls `release()` on the guarded fetch). Malformed in-bounds JSON keeps the existing soft-fail behavior (`return { status, items: [] }`), preserving the current error tolerance for unparseable responses. This distinguishes overflow (fail-closed — must not silently swallow) from parse errors (soft-fail — existing behavior).

**Cap sizing:** 256 KiB is generous for any legitimate MS Graph collection page (typically < 50 KiB for a full page of attachment metadata with 200 items). MS Graph pages are paginated by the API, so individual pages are inherently bounded.

**Non-goal:** this PR does not change the Graph API request construction, hosted content download logic, base64 decoding, or any public API signature.

## User Impact

MS Teams Graph collection reads are now protected from an OOM crash triggered by an oversized API response. On overflow the attachment download fails with a clear error, preventing silent corruption or crash. Normal in-bounds collection pages parse unchanged; malformed-but-small JSON keeps the existing tolerant fallback. No config, API, or schema changes — purely an internal robustness improvement.

## Evidence

### Existing tests

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-msteams.config.ts extensions/msteams/src/attachments/graph.test.ts

 ✓ fetches $value endpoint when contentBytes is null but item.id exists
 ✓ skips hosted content when contentBytes is null and id is missing
 ✓ skips $value content when Content-Length exceeds maxBytes
 ✓ uses inline contentBytes when available instead of $value
 ✓ adds the OpenClaw User-Agent to guarded Graph attachment fetches
 ✓ adds the OpenClaw User-Agent to Graph shares downloads for reference attachments
 ✓ does NOT call the nonexistent /attachments sub-resource
 ✓ sources reference attachments from the message body's attachments array
 ✓ logs a debug event when the message fetch throws instead of swallowing it
 ✓ logs a debug event when the message fetch returns non-ok
 ✓ logs a debug event when token acquisition fails

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  11 passed (11)
```

All 11 existing tests pass unchanged, confirming the bounded read does not regress the Graph attachment download path.

### Design verification

The bounded read is positioned OUTSIDE the existing JSON-parse `try/catch`:
- **Overflow:** `readResponseWithLimit` throws → propagates through outer `try/finally` → `release()` called → error reaches caller (fail-closed)
- **Malformed in-bounds JSON:** `JSON.parse` throws → caught by inner `catch` → returns `{status, items: []}` (existing soft-fail behavior preserved)
- **Normal responses:** parse and return unchanged

This is the correct fail-closed design: overflow must not be silently folded into the empty-items fallback.

### Lint

`oxlint --quiet` is clean (exit 0) on the changed file.

### Mutation check (change is load-bearing)

Temporarily moving the bounded read inside the inner `try/catch` would silently swallow overflow into `{status, items: []}` — confirming the placement guards the fail-closed boundary and cannot be simplified away.

<details>
<summary>Security and Privacy</summary>

- Hardening fix: removes an unbounded-memory read of an external (MS Graph) response, closing a DoS/OOM vector reachable via a compromised or MITM'd endpoint.
- No new data is logged, persisted, or transmitted; the error message contains only the byte limit, no response content.
- No new dependency — reuses the existing `openclaw/plugin-sdk/response-limit-runtime` helper.
- Fail-closed for overflow: oversized input is rejected rather than silently treated as an empty collection.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Compatibility</summary>

- Backwards compatible for all normal-size responses: the collection item extraction and attachment processing are unchanged.
- Only oversized (>256 KiB) collection pages change outcome (now fail closed). 256 KiB is ~5× larger than any legitimate MS Graph collection page.
- No API, config, or schema changes. Blast radius is low: a single source file, no shared infra/mocks touched.

</details>

---

AI-assisted (Claude Code). Implementation and tests were authored with Claude Code (Anthropic). Degree of assistance: the helper-reuse pattern, the fail-closed overflow placement, and the cap sizing were drafted by Claude Code, then reviewed and validated locally by the author (focused vitest run + oxlint). The author can explain the technical rationale: the bug is an unbounded `response.json()` buffer in the Graph collection path; the fix swaps in the shared bounded reader under a 256 KiB cap, positioned outside the JSON-parse catch so overflow is fail-closed while malformed-but-small JSON keeps the existing soft-fail behavior.

target.title: security: gateway public network hardening
target.body:
## Summary

Implements comprehensive security hardening for OpenClaw Gateway when exposed to public networks (e.g. `https://openclaw.allegro.earth/`). The existing security mechanisms (non-loopback auth enforcement, auth rate limiting, CORS checks) leave gaps that this PR addresses:

- **IP access control** (allowlist/blocklist with CIDR support) — enforced on both HTTP requests and WebSocket upgrades, loopback always allowed, blocklist takes priority
- **Password/token strength validation** — CRITICAL startup warnings when network-exposed with short tokens (<32 chars) or weak passwords (<12 chars, all-digit/all-letter patterns)
- **TLS enforcement check** — CRITICAL startup warning when network-exposed without TLS and no `terminatedUpstream` declaration
- **Per-IP request rate limiting** — sliding window (default 120 req/min/IP), loopback exempt by default, returns 429 with Retry-After
- **Auth audit logging** — JSONL to `~/.openclaw/logs/gateway-auth.jsonl` with file rotation, records `auth_failure`, `auth_success`, `rate_limited`, `ip_blocked` events
- **Auto HSTS** — `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000` set automatically when TLS is enabled
- **Eliminate silent 0.0.0.0 fallback** — `loopback`, `tailnet`, and `custom` bind modes now throw clear errors instead of silently falling back to all-interfaces
- **New security audit checks** — `gateway.no_tls_network_exposed` (critical), `gateway.password_too_short` (critical), `gateway.password_weak_pattern` (warn), `gateway.no_request_rate_limit` (warn), `gateway.auto_bind_fallback` (warn)
- **Enhanced `doctor` warnings** — TLS, password strength, token length, request rate limit checks for network-exposed gateways

### Config additions (`gateway.*`)

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `ipAllowlist` | `string[]` | — | CIDR/IP allowlist (loopback always allowed) |
| `ipBlocklist` | `string[]` | — | CIDR/IP blocklist (checked before allowlist) |
| `requestRateLimit.maxRequests` | `number` | 120 | Max requests per IP per window |
| `requestRateLimit.windowMs` | `number` | 60000 | Sliding window duration (ms) |
| `requestRateLimit.exemptLoopback` | `boolean` | true | Skip rate limiting for localhost |
| `tls.terminatedUpstream` | `boolean` | false | Declare TLS terminated by reverse proxy |
